ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Analysis of Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation Methods for Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We will compare and evaluate 5 state-of-the-art episodic and 5 state-of-the-art online TTA methods on 3 Vision-Language models (LLaMA, ALBERT-ViT, and ViLT), across 5 real-world benchmarks (VisualGenome, iNaturalist, COCO/ Captions, VQA v2, and LC-STS), using accuracy as the primary metric. We will also replicate and reproduce the reported baseline results of each TTA method to establish a fair and controlled comparison.
CONTROLS: Baseline: unadapted models, Pre-trained models: CLIP, No adaptation, Text prompts: original prompts used in the TTA methods
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvements over the unadapted model of 2-5% on average, with some TTA methods showing negligible improvement due to varying他们pre-trained models and evaluation protocols.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness and Trustworthiness of Test-Time Adaptation Methods for Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We will extend the experiments in proposal 1 by evaluating the robustness and trustworthiness of the adapted models using rigorous testing protocols, such as adversarial attacks (PGD, FGSM), the distribution of shifts (data augmentation), calibration metrics (NLL, ECE), and convergence speed on a stream of test data.
CONTROLS: Baseline: unadapted models, Proposal 1
COST: 500 GPU-hours (adds to proposal 1)
PREDICTION: Expected improvements in robustness and trustworthiness for plain adaptation methods such as episode adaptation for vision-language.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Pre-Training on the Performance of Test-Time Adaptation Methods for Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of different pre-trained models (e.g., ViLT, ViLBERT, DETR, SWIN, SwIN-T, SwIN-B, SwIN-L) on the performance of TTA methods, comparing standard ImageNet-pretrained and self-supervised pre-trained models, and examining how these differences impact the adaptation process.
CONTROLS: Baseline: CLIP, Proposal 1, Proposal 2
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement of up to 10% in performance when using pre-trained models with strong vision or language capabilities, but potential drop in performance for models that poorly generalize to the test data distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Generalizability of Test-Time Adaptation Methods Across Different Vision-Language Model Architectures and Tasks
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the generalizability of TTA methods across different VLM architectures (e.g., sequential and parallel) and task-specific models (e.g., VQA, NLVR2), as well as their adaptability to new tasks, using a set of transfer learning datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Proposal 1, Proposal 2 (on diverse VLM architectures), Proposal 3
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement of up to 5% in performance for task-agnostic models, but potential instability in adapting to new tasks, highlighting the need for task-specific models.

TITLE ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conclusion and Future Directions for Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: We will synthesize the findings from our previous experiments and theoretical results, identifying key directions for future research in test-time adaptation, including the need for better understanding of adaptation mechanisms and their interaction with task-specific features.
CONTROLS: All previous proposals
COST: negligible
PREDICTION: Expected to provide a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art in test-time adaptation methods and guide future research directions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Baseline Performance of CLIP and VIT for Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We conduct a thorough evaluation of CLIP and Vision Transformers (VIT) for image classification tasks, exploring the performance of both models with various fine-tuning schemes (fine-tuning the entire model, adapter-based fine-tuning, and prompt-based fine-tuning) and evaluation metrics (accuracy, mean class precision, mean class recall).
CONTROLS: In addition to comparing different models and fine-tuning schemes, we also compare against a simple baseline model (e.g. a ResNet-50) and ablation experiments that remove specific layers or components from the VLMs to assess their impact on performance.
COST: 10-15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect CLIP to outperform VIT across all fine-tuning schemes and evaluation metrics due to its better multimodal alignment capabilities. However, we may find that prompt-based fine-tuning can lead to overfitting, particularly for smaller datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Recent Episodic TTA Methods on CLIP and VIT for Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We devise a controlled experiment to compare the performance of recent episodic TTA methods (e.g., Visual Prompt Learning, GeneVLP, and others) on CLIP and VIT for image classification tasks. We use the same fine-tuning schemes and evaluation metrics from our baseline experiment (item 1) to ensure fair comparisons. Additionally, we implement an episodic TTA method from scratch to demonstrate its competitiveness.
CONTROLS: To provide a fair comparison, we maintain the same model checkpoints, text prompts, evaluation protocols, and hyperparameters across all experiments. We also include ablation studies to assess the impact of specific components within the TTA methods.
COST: 30-40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect recent episodic TTA methods to achieve significant gains over the unadapted models, with CLIP typically outperforming VIT. However, we anticipate variations in performance across different TTA methods and datasets, highlighting the need for further research to identify the most effective approaches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparison of Episodic and Online TTA Methods for CLIP-based Image Captioning
PROPOSAL: We investigate the application of both episodic and online TTA methods on CLIP for image captioning, evaluating their performance on a diverse set of image captioning datasets (e.g., COCO, MSCOCO, and others). We use the same CLIP model checkpoint and fine-tuning scheme from our baseline experiment, adapting the TTA methods for the image captioning task.
CONTROLS: To ensure fairness and provide a clear understanding of the TTA methods' effectiveness, we compare against the unadapted CLIP model, a simple baseline model (e.g., a Transformer-based captioning model), and ablation studies to remove specific components from the TTA methods.
COST: 20-30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect online TTA methods to demonstrate greater gains over episodic TTA methods, particularly for captioning tasks requiring longer context and more nuanced understanding. However, the effectiveness of online TTA may be compromised if the adaptation does not generalize well across varying image captions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Image Captioning as a Secondary Task on CLIP and VIT
PROPOSAL: We modify our previous experiment (item 3) and use the CLIP-based image captioning model to investigate whether training image classification and image captioning concurrently can lead to improved adaptation performance in CLIP, comparing against the baseline model and individual fine-tuning of each task.
CONTROLS: We include ablation studies to assess the impact of captioning task strength, captioning loss coefficients, and gradient reversal on adaptation performance. Additionally, we compare against the unadapted models and a simple baseline model.
COST: 25-35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the dual-task fine-tuning approach to improve adaptation performance, particularly for tasks requiring nuanced understanding, by leveraging the image captioning task to aggressively adapt CLIP to the test domain. However, the additional complexity might compromise the adaptation's ability to generalize across varying image classification tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Robustness of Test-Time Adaptation Against Distribution Shifts
PROPOSAL: We assess the performance of recent episodic and online TTA methods (item 2) on CLIP and VIT under distribution shifts, where the test data follows a different distribution compared to the training data. This is achieved by introducing label noise, corruption of input data, or using a different dataset for testing. We evaluate the models' robustness to these shifts using metrics such as classification accuracy, AUC-ROC, and robust accuracy.
CONTROLS: We compare the TTA methods against a set of robustness baselines, including the unadapted models and simple robustness training methods like data augmentation and adversarial training.
COST: 15-25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the robustness of TTA methods to be lower than the unadapted models when faced with distribution shifts, as they adapt to the specific domain but neglect the underlying distribution. However, we anticipate significant improvements in robust accuracy when using more robust adaptation methods, such as those that incorporate generative models or adversarial training.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Recent Episodic TTA Methods on CLIP and VIT Beyond Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We broaden the scope of our experiment (item 2) and evaluate the recent episodic TTA methods on a wider range of tasks, including object detection (e.g., COCO), semantic segmentation (e.g., Cityscapes), and multi-modal retrieval (e.g., Flickr30k). This allows us to investigate the transferability of TTA methods across different tasks.
CONTROLS: We maintain the same experimental setup and evaluation metrics as our previous experiment, comparing the TTA methods against the unadapted models and including ablation studies to remove specific components from the TTA methods.
COST: 40-50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the TTA methods to demonstrate varying degrees of transferability across different tasks, with stronger performance gains observed in tasks with more similar domains and adaptation requirements. However, we anticipate significant challenges in adapting TTA methods to tasks with distinct requirements, such as object detection and semantic segmentation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Overfitting in Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of overfitting in TTA by deriving bounds on the expected generalization error and exploring the effect of adaptation on the Hessian matrix of the model. This analysis will provide insights into the inherent challenges of adapting models at test time, such as overfitting, and help identify potential strategies to alleviate these issues.
CONTROLS: We will assume a simple adaptation scenario where the test data is drawn from the same underlying distribution as the training data, and analyze the behavior of TTA methods in this idealized setting.
COST: 5-10 CPU-days
PREDICTION: We expect our theoretical analysis to reveal the fundamental limitations of TTA methods in terms of overfitting, and identify key factors that contribute to this phenomenon. However, we anticipate that the analysis will also uncover potential vulnerabilities in certain adaptation strategies, highlighting the need for further research to develop more robust and effective TTA methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Test-Time Adaptation on Model Explanability
PROPOSAL: We explore the effect of TTA methods on the explainability of CLIP and VIT models, evaluating the extent to which adaptation modifies the model's features and decision boundaries. We use techniques such as saliency maps, feature importance, and SHAP values to assess the model's interpretability before and after adaptation.
CONTROLS: We compare the explainability of the adapted models against the unadapted models and include ablation studies to remove specific components from the TTA methods and assess their impact on explainability.
COST: 20-30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect TTA methods to compromise model explainability by adapting to the test data and modifying the model's internal representations. However, we anticipate that the adaptation may also reveal new insights into the model's decision-making process, highlighting the need for further research to develop more interpretable adaptation strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Transferability of Test-Time Adaptation Across VLM Architectures
PROPOSAL: We investigate the transferability of TTA methods across different VLM architectures, evaluating the extent to which the adaptation observed in one model can be transferred to another. We compare the performance of TTA methods on CLIP, VIT, and other popular VLM architectures, and explore the factors that contribute to the transferability of adaptation.
CONTROLS: We include ablation studies to remove specific components from the TTA methods and assess their impact on transferability, and compare the transferability of adaptation across different VLM architectures.
COST: 30-40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the transferability of adaptation to vary across different VLM architectures, with some architectures being more adaptable than others. However, we anticipate that the adaptation can be transferred to some extent across different architectures, highlighting the need for further research to develop more robust and transferable adaptation strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Case Study: Real-World Deployment of Test-Time Adaptation for Multimodal Retrieval
PROPOSAL: We conduct a case study to evaluate the effectiveness of TTA methods in a real-world deployment scenario for multimodal retrieval tasks. We collect a diverse dataset of images and text from a social media platform, and evaluate the performance of several TTA methods in adapting to the platform's unique characteristics and potentially noisy data.
CONTROLS: We include ablation studies to assess the impact of specific components from the TTA methods and the adapting to the platform's characteristics on the overall performance. We also compare the TTA methods against a baseline model that has been trained on the platform's data.
COST: 50-60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the TTA methods to demonstrate significant improvements in performance over the baseline model, particularly in terms of adaptability and accuracy. However, we anticipate that the real-world deployment scenario may introduce additional challenges and complexities that can affect the performance of the TTA methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consistent Baseline Reproductions for Episodic and Online TTA Methods
PROPOSAL: Reproduce baseline results for a variety of episodic and online TTA methods under consistent experimental settings using CLIP as the pre-trained model, standardizing the prompt, checkpoint, and evaluation protocol. Specifically, we will use the SimCLR-V2 and Faster R-CNN checkpoints, the provided text prompts for image classification and retrieval tasks, and the standard COCO validation set for evaluation. This will allow for fair comparisons between existing methods and assess the true amount of progress made.
CONTROLS: We will control for the choice of pre-trained model checkpoint, text prompts, and evaluation protocol by ensuring these are consistent across all experiments.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With consistent experimental settings, we expect to reproduce the reported results of existing episodic and online TTA methods, and assess the gap between them and the unadapted CLIP model. However, it's possible that the promised gains of recent methods over earlier ones are exaggerated due to variability in experimental settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Test-Time Adaptation on Diverse VLM Architectures
PROPOSAL: Examine the effectiveness of both episodic and online test-time adaptation methods on a range of VLM architectures, including CONV-BERT, ViLBERT, and LXMERT, to assess the generalizability of existing TTA methods. We will use a similar set-up as the consistent baseline reproductions (proposal 1) and report results on a variety of tasks such as image classification, retrieval, and captioning.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results of existing TTA methods on CLIP (proposal 1) to those on the alternative VLM architectures, and use the same set of tasks and evaluation metrics to ensure fair comparisons.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the existing TTA methods will exhibit varying levels of effectiveness on the different VLM architectures, with potential trade-offs between performance and computational cost. However, it's possible that some of the TTA methods will struggle to generalize across architectures, limiting their practical utility.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Test-Time Adaptation on Diverse VLM Architectures
REVISION: Modify proposal 2 to add a comparison between the test-time adaptation methods and training-time fine-tuning of the VLM architectures on the same tasks. This will help evaluate whether test-time adaptation is a complementary or conflicting technique to traditional fine-tuning methods.
CONTROLS: We will use the same set-up as before (proposal 2) and compare the results of test-time adaptation to those of training-time fine-tuning on the same tasks and evaluation metrics.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (additional 20 GPU-hours for fine-tuning)
PREDICTION: We expect to see that test-time adaptation and training-time fine-tuning have different strengths and weaknesses, and that test-time adaptation will be particularly useful when fine-tuning is not feasible due to lack of annotated data or computational resources. However, some methods may show conflicting results, highlighting the need for more research in this area.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Test-Time Adaptation on Diverse VLM Architectures
REVISION: Modify the task list for proposal 2 to include not only image classification, retrieval, and captioning but also more nuanced tasks that assess the model's robustness and trustworthiness, such as out-of-distribution detection and adversarial robustness.
CONTROLS: We will use the same set-up as before (proposal 2) and compare the results of test-time adaptation to those of training-time fine-tuning (for some of these tasks) on the same tasks and evaluation metrics, with the exception of adversarial robustness.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (no additional cost for out-of-distribution detection)
PREDICTION: We expect to see that test-time adaptation not only improves the accuracy of the model but also its robustness and trustworthiness, particularly for out-of-distribution detection. However, some methods may show conflicting results on adversarial robustness, indicating the need for further research in this area.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Test-Time Adaptation on Diverse VLM Architectures
PROPOSAL: Examine the effectiveness of both episodic and online test-time adaptation methods on a range of VLM architectures, including CONV-BERT, ViLBERT, and LXMERT, to assess the generalizability of existing TTA methods. Specifically, we will employ the following nuanced tasks to evaluate the trustworthiness of the adapted models: out-of-distribution detection (OOD-Det), robustness to adversarial attacks (Adv-Robust), and multi-modal evaluation of semantic similarity (Multi-Modal Semantic Similarity).
CONTROLS: We will compare the results of existing TTA methods on CLIP (proposal 1) to those on the alternative VLM architectures, and use the same set-up as before (proposal 2).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the existing TTA methods will demonstrate varying levels of effectiveness across the different VLM architectures and nuanced tasks, revealing opportunities for further research and refinement. However, some TTA methods may struggle with OOD-Det and Adv-Robust, indicating the need for more resilient adaptation strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Test-Time Adaptation on Default and Perceptual Metrics
PROPOSAL: Assess the influence of test-time adaptation methods on default accuracy-oriented metrics (e.g., classification accuracy) versus perceptual metrics (e.g., image quality, semantic similarity) to better understand the trade-offs and potential side effects of adaptation. For this evaluation, we will use a set of automated metrics that assess image and caption quality, semantic similarity, and other perceptually relevant factors.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results of test-time adaptation on CLIP (proposal 1) to those of training-time fine-tuning on the standard metrics as well as the proposed perceptual metrics.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that test-time adaptation improves default accuracy-oriented metrics but may compromise perceptual metrics, particularly when dealing with nuanced or rare cases. However, some TTA methods may exhibit improved performance across both types of metrics, leading to more robust and trustworthy models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Robustness of Test-Time Adaptation to Perturbations and Out-of-Multimodal Domain Transfer
PROPOSAL: Examine the robustness of test-time adaptation methods to input perturbations (e.g., noise, blur) and out-of-multimodal domain transfer scenarios (e.g., applicability to novel visual-text combinations). This will help identify potential weaknesses and opportunities for improvement in the current TTA methods.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of TTA methods under the specified perturbation scenarios and domain transfer conditions using both controlled simulations and real-world benchmarks.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that test-time adaptation will generally be less robust to input perturbations and out-of-multimodal domain transfer scenarios, likely due to the difficulty of disentangling task-specific and task-agnostic knowledge during adaptation. However, some TTA methods may exhibit resilience or even benefits in certain configurations, leading to new avenues for exploration and improvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Time Complexity Analysis of Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Investigate the computational complexity of existing test-time adaptation methods and their implications for practical deployment in real-time applications. We will analyze the time and computational resources required for each TTA method, exploring their scalability and potential bottlenecks.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of TTA methods in a real-time simulation environment, simulating different loading scenarios and available computational resources.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that test-time adaptation methods not requiring iterative optimization will offer advantages in terms of responsiveness and resource efficiency. However, the true bottlenecks may arise during fine-grained analysis of large datasets or textual prompts, necessitating adaptations of trusted optimization techniques to mitigate the time complexity of TTA.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Case Studies of Real-World Deployment and Usage of Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Conduct a qualitative analysis of the challenges and limitations of deploying test-time adaptation methods in real-world applications, involving both professional end-users and novice practitioners. We will gather insights through survey responses, interviews, and anonymized logs of online usage.
CONTROLS: We will use a stratified sampling approach to gather data from various user demographics and ensure a balanced view of the pros and cons of TTA.
COST: 20 hours of human-annotated data collection
PREDICTION: We expect that while test-time adaptation offers significant flexibility and real-time capabilities, its practical deployment will face challenges related to engineering simpler error explanations and diagnostic tools for models in complex, real-world use cases. Respondents might also perceive existing TTA methods as being too difficult to use or remember.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Analysis of Test-Time Adaptation's Impact on VLM Performance and Real-World Deployment
PROPOSAL: Integrate the findings from the previous studies into a comprehensive meta-analysis to identify overarching trends, correlations, and contradictions in the performance of test-time adaptation methods across different scenarios. This will enable the derivation of key insights and recommendations for the future development and application of test-time adaptation techniques in vision-language research.
CONTROLS: We will create data duplication-free datasets and use generalized linear combination models to generate the final confidence intervals that offset false discovery through study replications or variations.
COST: 50 hours of analysis work, requiring no additional computational resources
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our final, high level, resource-efficient discussion will substantiate test-time adaptation as a promising approach to manage complexity, regarding a pressing need for verifiability in almost all highly interacting information flows, according to workflow piece-wise efficiency while similarly devised algorithms didn't make their applicability to VLM mainly due to technique-vis equilibrium being tricky.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fair Comparison of Episodic TTA Methods on CLIP
PROPOSAL: Perform an exhaustive comparison of 5 recent episodic TTA methods on CLIP with a common set of evaluation metrics, including accuracy, robustness, and fairness, on ImageNet and COCO datasets. This will involve re-implementing and tuning the methods using a single pre-trained CLIP model checkpoint and reporting results on two different text prompts: one with and one without class labels.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline of using the pre-trained CLIP model without any adaptation and also with a re-implementation of the first TTA method published in this area.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the recent episodic TTA methods will show stronger performance than the baseline model on both datasets, but possibly not more than a 5% reduction in error rate. All methods will show some degree of test-time adaptation gain, with disagreement on the best-performing method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Online TTA Methods on CLIP
PROPOSAL: Evaluate 8 online TTA methods with a focus on test-time fairness and robustness on a diverse set of real-world datasets, including CelebA, Cars, and Pet dataset. We will use two different adaptation schedules and two different text prompts with varying levels of ambiguity. We also compare the results with a baseline of using the pre-trained CLIP model without any adaptation and with an ensemble of multiple adaptations.
CONTROLS: Compare with the results of proposal 1 (Fair Comparison of Episodic TTA Methods on CLIP) to ensure that our findings are consistent with the episodic TTA methods.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Online TTA methods will demonstrate a trade-off between accuracy and fairness across the datasets, with some methods performing well on one metric but poorly on the other. We also anticipate that the ensemble adaptation will outperform all individual TTA methods.

Note: This proposal builds upon the first one by exploring another type of TTA and multiple evaluation aspects, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of the subject.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Online TTA Methods on CLIP (revision)
PROPOSAL: In addition to evaluating 8 online TTA methods on the CelebA, Cars, and Pet dataset, we also explore the extension of these methods to other VLM architectures beyond CLIP, such as DALL-E and VIT.
